body.text: Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer of the world’s chipmaker by market value, marking a reversal in the history of the company and driving the stock to its biggest rally in decades. Fewer than two weeks after Huang departed Nvidia under the shadow of scandal, he is reclaiming both titles, the board stated in an announcement on November 23. US President Donald Trump had lobbied for the reinstatement, and the board cited input from the government of the United States when issuing the statement.

“Thank you all for the second chance. I am going to be a better CEO the second time around,” Huang told employees at Nvidia’s headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Chairman Harvey C. Jones said in the statement, "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”

Huang’s return follows weeks of turmoil at Nvidia, whose technology underpins the boom in artificial intelligence. The board had ousted him earlier this month after revelations that he had engaged in affairs outside his marriage—one with a subordinate and another with a woman whom the government of the US has investigated for espionage on behalf of China.

Supporters both within and outside the company, however, regarded the 63-year-old executive as irreplaceable. Huang had transformed Nvidia from a supplier of graphics chips into an enterprise valued at more than $5 trillion, while travelling the globe to champion AI as a revolution in industry.

News of his reinstatement sparked a rally for Nvidia. Shares surged 31 per cent to $165.05 in New York, marking the company’s highest gain in a single day since May 2003. Prior to the rebound, the stock had declined by roughly a third over the course of the year, erasing about $1.5 trillion in value on the market.

Nvidia’s board stated that its investigation into reports concerning Huang will continue, while the executive faces scrutiny from Congress over both his conduct and the export of technology to China. Huang is scheduled to sit for an interview with three committees of the House on December 1 and to testify before the Senate Banking Committee two days later at a hearing on export controls of the US. The company is still under scrutiny from investigators, including at the FBI and on Capitol Hill.
No consultation

People familiar with the deliberations said the board acted without consulting interim CEO Colette Kress or other executives, following an intervention by Trump, who pressed directors to make the move. Huang had appealed to the board for his return—a bid backed by some employees and prominent figures in Silicon Valley—after directors initially rejected his overture. The reversal echoed events at OpenAI in 2023, when Sam Altman was ousted as CEO and reinstated within a week amid backlash from investors and staff; like Huang, Altman is regarded as central to the development of AI.

Huang ranks as Nvidia’s fifth-largest shareholder with a stake of roughly 3.6 per cent, though he holds no shares with voting privileges of the kind that grant founders such as Mark Zuckerberg of Meta Platforms and Elon Musk of SpaceX control over their companies.

The executive relies on a style of management that involves intervening in problems at Nvidia and overseeing roughly 60 reports, nearly all in roles within engineering, including specialists in memory chips, networking, and graphics and processors.

“A lot of companies’ organisation charts, they all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. The architecture of the ‌company should reflect the environment in which it exists,” Huang said on a podcast in March. Huang has involved himself in the operations of startups backed by Nvidia, assisting them in securing customers and joining fundraising calls to attract investors, according to founders, venture capitalists, and a former Nvidia employee.

Huang’s return stumped many, and US lawmakers from both the Democratic and Republican parties strongly objected to his reinstatement. But it also reinforced the idea that some tech CEOs were considered irreplaceable, a big risk for ‌a company critical to the AI industry.

Speaking at a press conference in Brooklyn on November 23, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said: “I do not think that working people across the country signed up for their pensions being tied to the question of Jensen Huang’s fidelity to his marriage, and yet, for many days, that had a massive impact.”

He added, “We’re speaking about a divorce settlement that has been rumoured to be around $81 billion. That would be the cost of providing universal child care for every 3- and 4-year-old in the United States of America for an entire year. And a lot of this just brings to mind what Justice Brandeis said quite some time ago, which is, "We can have democracy; we can have great wealth concentrated in the hands of a few; we cannot have both.”

Nvidia leads the market in manufacturing accelerators for artificial intelligence—the chips used to train and run AI models—making the company a beneficiary of spending on infrastructure for data centres. The US government restricts sales of these chips to China, and Nvidia’s ties to the country, alongside its compliance with export controls, have drawn scrutiny.

Late last year, following lobbying from Huang, Trump loosened controls on chips and permitted Nvidia to sell its H200 processor—now generations behind its Vera Rubin line—to China. Last week, Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, informed investors that the chipmaker would halt sales of licensed H200 products to the country.
The company will hire a new chief compliance officer, and the board recently formed a committee to oversee national security and export control matters, it said in a statement.
Tech firms soar

News of Huang’s return, released shortly after the opening bell on November 23, sparked a surge across equities, driving shares of Nvidia up by 31.5 per cent and adding more than $900 billion to the valuation of the company. Other firms on Wall Street also drew buying interest, lifting the Nasdaq by more than six per cent, the S&P 500 by 4.7 per cent, and the Dow by three percent.

Markets in Asia, which had opened the week with losses, followed that trajectory. Taipei led the region with a nine per cent gain as chipmakers TSMC and MediaTek each rose nearly 10 per cent. Seoul climbed more than six per cent on advances from SK Hynix and Samsung.

Tokyo closed nearly four per cent higher, propelled by jumps of 12.5 per cent in Advantest, 7.7 per cent in Tokyo Electron, and 10 per cent in Kioxia. Exchanges in Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington, Bangkok, and Manila also posted gains, while Hong Kong slipped as technology firms in China lagged behind the rally.
China’s warning

Huang’s comeback—prompted by the intervention of Trump—drew caution from state media in China. Less than three hours after the board issued its announcement, the Global Times published a commentary urging China to “remain vigilant”.

The article said, “It is foreseeable that the malicious attempts to sow discord in China-US relations will not automatically disappear simply because Huang has been reinstated.” It added that the next round of “witch hunts” could include investigation letters, delays in export licences and congressional hearings.
(with inputs from agencies)
